title: Assembly
tagline: x86-64 assembly: talk to the processor directly
description: Write programs in the processor's own instructions: x86-64 assembly in Intel syntax with NASM, running on Linux. Starting from a program that prints with a system call, the course covers registers, data, Xenon's print and read routines, arithmetic, multiplying and dividing, bit operations and the flags, how numbers become printed digits, compares and jumps, loops, signed and unsigned conditions, if and switch as the compiler writes them, branch-free code, addressing modes, arrays, strings, the stack, buffers and input, call and ret, the System V calling convention, stack frames, recursion, calling and being called from C, reading compiler output, parsing numbers, optimisation, SIMD, ARM64, and finally floating point with SSE, NASM macros, files through system calls, structures, and bit scanning and atomic instructions, then string instructions, division by magic numbers, jump tables, memory from mmap, and arguments and the environment. Every lesson has checked practice, assembled with NASM and run for real, and every milestone ends with five projects, from small to large.

milestones.title: Hello, Machine
milestones.blurb: What assembly is, registers, mov and exit codes, system calls, data, and Xenon's print and read routines.

lessons.title: What Assembly Is
lessons.summary: A processor runs machine code - numbers that each mean one small instruction. Assembly gives every instruction a name, and an assembler turns the names back into the numbers. This course writes x86-64 assembly in Intel syntax with NASM, for Linux. A program has sections for data and code, labels that name addresses, and starts at _start.

lessons.title: Registers
lessons.summary: Registers are the processor's own tiny, fast storage - sixteen 64-bit general-purpose ones on x86-64, plus rip (the next instruction) and rflags. The low 32, 16 and 8 bits of each have their own names, such as eax, ax and al. Writing a 32-bit register clears the top half of the 64-bit one; writing 8 or 16 bits does not.

lessons.title: mov and Exit Codes
lessons.summary: mov copies a value into a register - a constant, another register, or (later) memory. Both sides must be the same size. A program's exit code is the number it hands to the exit system call, and it is the simplest way to see a result. xor of a register with itself is the usual way to set it to 0.

lessons.title: System Calls write and exit
lessons.summary: A program cannot touch the screen, files or the keyboard itself - it asks the operating system with the syscall instruction. On Linux the call's number goes in rax and its arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8 and r9, and the result comes back in rax. write (1) prints bytes, read (0) reads them, exit (60) ends the program.

lessons.title: Data db, dw, dd, dq and equ
lessons.summary: db, dw, dd and dq put 1, 2, 4 and 8-byte values into the program, stored little-endian. A label is just the address of the next byte, $ is the current address, and equ names a constant such as a length. times repeats, .bss reserves zeroed space with resb and resq, and .rodata holds data that must not change.

lessons.title: Xenon's Print and Read Routines
lessons.summary: Turning a number into printed digits takes a loop and a division, which come later in the course. Until then, Xenon adds ready-made routines to any program that calls them - print_str, print_int, print_hex, print_bin, print_newline, read_int, read_char and read_line. Put the argument in rdi (and rsi), call, and expect rax, rcx, rdx, rsi, rdi and r8 to r11 to change.

milestones.title: Arithmetic and Logic
milestones.blurb: Adding and subtracting, multiplying and dividing, bit instructions and shifts, the flags, and how a number is printed.

lessons.title: add, sub, inc, dec and neg
lessons.summary: add and sub combine two operands into the first, inc and dec add or take away one, and neg flips the sign. Results wrap around at the register's size, so 32-bit arithmetic wraps at 2 to the 32 and also clears the upper half. The same add instruction serves signed and unsigned numbers, because two's complement makes them the same bits.

lessons.title: Multiplying and Dividing
lessons.summary: imul multiplies with two or three operands and keeps the low bits of the answer. div and idiv divide the 128-bit number in rdx:rax by an operand, leaving the quotient in rax and the remainder in rdx - so rdx must be prepared first, with xor for unsigned and cqo for signed. Dividing by zero stops the program.

lessons.title: Bit Instructions and Shifts
lessons.summary: and, or, xor and not work on every bit at once and make masks for testing, setting and clearing bits. shl and shr shift bits left and right - multiplying and dividing unsigned numbers by powers of two - while sar keeps the sign for signed numbers. rol and ror rotate, a variable shift count goes in cl, and lea multiplies by 3, 5 and 9 in one step.

lessons.title: The Flags
lessons.summary: Arithmetic and logic instructions record facts about their result in rflags - ZF when it is zero, SF when it is negative, CF when an unsigned result wrapped, OF when a signed result overflowed. cmp and test set flags without keeping a result. adc and sbb use the carry to work on numbers bigger than a register.

lessons.title: Printing Digits Yourself
lessons.summary: To print a number, split it into decimal digits with div - by 100 for the hundreds, by 10 for the tens, the remainder for the units - and turn each digit into a character by adding '0'. Store the characters in a buffer and write them. print_int does the same with a loop, building the digits from the right.

milestones.title: Control Flow
milestones.blurb: Compares and jumps, loops, signed and unsigned conditions, if and switch from C, and branch-free code.

lessons.title: Compare and Jump
lessons.summary: jmp always jumps to a label. A conditional jump such as je, jne, jl or jg jumps only when the flags say so, which usually means right after cmp or test. An if statement becomes a compare, a jump over the code that should not run, and a label. Labels starting with a dot are local to the label above them.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.summary: A loop is a jump backwards. Counting loops often count down to zero with dec and jnz, since dec sets the zero flag for free. A while loop tests at the top and a do-while at the bottom; compilers prefer the bottom test with one check in front. Reading until read_int reports the end of the input makes a loop over all the input.

lessons.title: Signed and Unsigned Conditions
lessons.summary: The same bits compare differently as signed and unsigned numbers - all 1s is -1 or the largest number. cmp sets flags for both readings, and you choose with the jump - jl, jg for signed, jb, ja for unsigned. Using the wrong one is a classic bug, and one unsigned compare can check a whole range.

lessons.title: if, else and switch from C
lessons.summary: Chains of if and else become a series of compares, each jumping to the next test. && jumps out at the first false part and || at the first true part. A switch over close-together values becomes a jump table - an array of addresses indexed by the value - after one unsigned compare that sends everything out of range to default.

lessons.title: Branch-Free Code cmov and setcc
lessons.summary: Processors guess which way each jump will go and work ahead; a wrong guess wastes many cycles. cmovcc copies a value only if a condition holds, and setcc turns a condition into a 0 or 1 byte, so simple choices need no jump at all. Compilers use them for min, max, abs and boolean results.

milestones.title: Memory
milestones.blurb: Addressing modes, arrays, strings, the stack, and buffers for input.

lessons.title: Addressing Modes
lessons.summary: Square brackets mean memory. An address can be built from a base register, an index register times 1, 2, 4 or 8, and a constant, or relative to rip for labels. The size comes from the register or is written as byte, word, dword or qword. movzx and movsx widen small values, and lea computes an address without reading it.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.summary: An array in assembly is an address and a count - nothing marks its end or its type. Loop with an index and a scaled address, or move a pointer along by the element size until it reaches the end. Arrays come from the data section, .bss, or the caller, and the code must know whether each element is 1, 4 or 8 bytes.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.summary: A string is bytes in memory, ending with a 0 byte by C's convention. Loops over strings read one byte at a time with movzx and stop at the 0. Length, copy, compare and case changes are all short loops. The string instructions rep movsb and rep stosb copy and fill whole blocks in one instruction.

lessons.title: The Stack push and pop
lessons.summary: The stack is memory that grows downwards from a high address, and rsp always points at its top. push moves rsp down 8 bytes and stores a value; pop loads it and moves rsp back up. It saves registers that must be kept, holds temporary space reserved with sub rsp, and must end exactly where it started.

lessons.title: Buffers and Input
lessons.summary: Input arrives as bytes in a buffer, from the read system call or the read_line routine. Turning typed digits into a number is the reverse of printing - multiply what you have by 10 and add the next digit. Always pass the buffer's size, check what came back, and handle the end of the input.

milestones.title: Functions
milestones.blurb: call and ret, the System V calling convention, stack frames, recursion, and working with C.

lessons.title: call and ret
lessons.summary: call pushes the address of the next instruction onto the stack and jumps to the function; ret pops that address back into rip. That is all a function call is. Because the return address lives on the stack, a function must pop exactly what it pushed before ret, and functions can call other functions as deep as the stack allows.

lessons.title: The System V Calling Convention
lessons.summary: Linux and macOS follow the System V AMD64 convention. Integer and pointer arguments go in rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8 and r9, the rest on the stack, and the result comes back in rax. rbx, rbp, rsp and r12 to r15 must survive a call; everything else may be changed. rsp must be a multiple of 16 at every call.

lessons.title: Stack Frames and Locals
lessons.summary: A function's stack frame holds its return address, saved registers and local variables. The classic prologue pushes rbp and copies rsp into it, so locals sit at fixed offsets like [rbp - 8] however the stack moves; the epilogue undoes it with leave and ret. Optimised code often skips rbp and addresses locals from rsp.

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.summary: A recursive function calls itself, and each call has its own frame, so it works like any other call - as long as values needed after the inner call are saved first. Every level costs stack space, a base case stops the descent, and recursion too deep runs off the end of the stack and crashes.

lessons.title: Working with C
lessons.summary: Assembly functions that follow the calling convention can be called from C, and C functions from assembly, using global and extern and a linker. int values live in the low 32 bits with undefined upper bits. Windows x64 uses rcx, rdx, r8 and r9 with 32 bytes of shadow space and different saved registers. GCC's inline asm puts single instructions inside C.

milestones.title: Real Programs
milestones.blurb: Reading compiler output, parsing and printing numbers, optimisation, SIMD, and ARM64.

lessons.title: Reading Compiler Output
lessons.summary: Compiler output follows recognisable patterns. Leaf functions have no frame, xor zeroes, lea does arithmetic, and test, setcc and cmov replace branches. Division by a constant becomes a multiplication by a magic reciprocal, loops are rotated with one test in front, and simple loops over arrays are vectorised to work on 16 bytes at a time.

lessons.title: Parsing and Printing Numbers
lessons.summary: Now you can write the routines you have been borrowing. Parsing skips spaces, reads an optional sign, and multiplies and adds digit by digit, with any base and an overflow check. Printing divides by the base to produce digits from the right, handles the sign and the most negative number, and maps digits above 9 to letters.

lessons.title: Optimisation Basics
lessons.summary: Speed depends less on how many instructions run than on what they wait for. Memory is far slower than registers and caches hide it only for data used together. Chains of dependent instructions cannot overlap, wrong branch guesses cost many cycles, and division is slow. Measure with rdtsc before and after every change.

lessons.title: SIMD Many Numbers at Once
lessons.summary: SIMD instructions do the same operation on several values at once. Every x86-64 processor has sixteen 128-bit xmm registers that hold 16 bytes, 8 words, 4 dwords or 2 qwords, with instructions like paddb, paddd and paddq. movdqu loads and stores 16 bytes, and a horizontal sum combines the lanes at the end. AVX widens this to 256 and 512 bits.

lessons.title: Beyond x86 ARM64 and Debuggers
lessons.summary: ARM64, in phones and Apple-chip Macs, is a load-store design with 31 registers and fixed 4-byte instructions, so arithmetic never touches memory directly. RISC-V is a small open design built on the same ideas. A debugger such as gdb steps through instructions and shows registers and memory, and objdump shows any program's machine code.

milestones.title: Deeper Assembly
milestones.blurb: Floating point with SSE, NASM macros and conditional assembly, files with system calls, structures and data layout, and bit scanning with atomic instructions.

lessons.title: Floating Point with SSE
lessons.summary: Doubles and floats in x86-64 - the xmm registers, movsd and movss, addsd, subsd, mulsd, divsd and sqrtsd, converting with cvtsi2sd, cvttsd2si and cvtsd2si, comparing with comisd and the flags it sets, constants in .data, and the calling convention for floating-point arguments and results.

tasks.title: Scale a list by a fraction

lessons.title: NASM Macros and Conditional Assembly
lessons.summary: Writing less assembly by hand - single-line macros with %define, multi-line macros with %macro and their parameters, local labels with %%, repeating code with %rep and %assign, choosing code with %if and %ifdef, and macros that generate whole functions.

tasks.title: Unrolled sums with a saving macro

lessons.title: Files with System Calls
lessons.summary: Working with files without any library - open with its flags and permission mode, read and write loops that handle partial transfers, close, lseek to move and to find a size, unlink, and reading errors from the negative value the kernel returns.

lessons.title: Structures and Data Layout
lessons.summary: Records in assembly - NASM's struc and endstruc for field offsets, istruc and at for initialised records, reaching fields through a pointer, arrays of structures and the index arithmetic they need, matching a C struct's layout and padding, and structure of arrays versus array of structures.

lessons.title: Bit Scanning and Atomics
lessons.summary: Instructions that work on single bits - popcnt, bsf, bsr, tzcnt and lzcnt, bt, bts, btr and btc - and the instructions behind every lock and atomic variable - the lock prefix, xadd, xchg and cmpxchg - with a compare-and-swap loop and a spinlock.

milestones.title: Assembly in Practice
milestones.blurb: String instructions, multiplying and dividing by constants without div, jump tables and function pointers, memory from the kernel with mmap, and command-line arguments and the environment.

lessons.title: String Instructions
lessons.summary: The x86 instructions built for blocks of memory - movsb, stosb, lodsb, scasb and cmpsb with rsi, rdi and rcx, the rep, repe and repne prefixes, the direction flag and cld, writing memcpy, memset, strlen and memcmp with them, and when a plain loop or SIMD is faster.

lessons.title: Multiplying and Dividing by Constants
lessons.summary: How compilers avoid slow instructions - multiplying by small constants with lea and shifts, dividing unsigned numbers by powers of two with shr, signed division by powers of two with a bias, replacing division by any constant with a multiply by a magic number and a shift, and computing remainders from the quotient.

tasks.title: Dividing by ten with a magic number

lessons.title: Jump Tables and Function Pointers
lessons.summary: Code addresses as data - a jump table that turns a switch into one bounds check and one indirect jump, tables of function addresses, calling through a register, passing a function to another function as a callback, and dispatching commands by number; with the bounds checks that keep indirect jumps safe.

tasks.title: A switch as a jump table
A calculator with a function table

lessons.title: Memory from the Kernel
lessons.summary: Getting memory at run time without a C library - the mmap system call with anonymous private pages, its six arguments and the flags that matter, errors as negative return values, munmap to give memory back, page sizes and rounding, the older brk call, and a bump allocator built on one mmap.

lessons.title: Command-Line Arguments and the Environment
lessons.summary: What a Linux program finds on its stack at _start - argc, the argv pointers and the zero that ends them, the environment strings after them, walking them in assembly, comparing a string prefix to find a variable such as HOME, turning arguments into numbers, and setting the exit code that scripts check.
